title: Guru Tegh Bahadur Stands at Delhi

title_i18n.en: Guru Tegh Bahadur Stands at Delhi

subtitle: Hind ki Chadar: The Quiet Sword of Conscience at Delhi
era: Ninth Guru and religious freedom, c. 1664-1675 CE
region: Anandpur Sahib, Delhi, Punjab, Bihar, Bengal and Assam
moral: Freedom of faith is worth defending even for others.

sources.citation: Bachittar Natak, attributed to Guru Gobind Singh, c. late 17th century
sources.note: Primary Sikh framing of Guru Tegh Bahadur's sacrifice.

sources.citation: Guru Granth Sahib, hymns and salokas of Guru Tegh Bahadur
sources.note: Direct evidence of his thought and devotional voice.

sources.citation: Louis E. Fenech, Martyrdom in the Sikh Tradition (2000); Satish Chandra, Medieval India (2001)
sources.note: Modern analysis of Sikh and Persian source conflicts.

panels.shot: solemn low-angle wide of Guru Tegh Bahadur standing calm before the distant domes of Delhi's imperial skyline

dialogue.text: Guru Tegh Bahadur, ninth Guru of the Sikhs, walks from Anandpur to Aurangzeb’s Delhi, choosing death rather than bend the conscience of India.

panels.shot: soft close-up on young Tyag Mal in a warrior encampment, lit by campfire glow

dialogue.text: Born Tyag Mal in 1621, son of Guru Hargobind, he grows in a world of swords and psalms, where the Sikh path has already taken up arms against Mughal power.

panels.shot: dynamic mid-shot of Tyag Mal in battle training, blurred motion of blade in foreground

dialogue.text: He learns to wield the sword but turns inward, more drawn to silence than to acclaim; in time he will be called Tegh Bahadur, the brave of the sword.

panels.shot: wide shot of the Ganga plain with Guru Tegh Bahadur walking among common folk

dialogue.text: Long before Delhi, he walks the dusty roads of Punjab, Bihar, Bengal and Assam, singing of fearlessness and detachment, building distant sangats far from court.

panels.shot: intimate close-up of the Guru seated in meditation, faint outline of Anandpur hills behind

dialogue.text: In 1664, he is named ninth Guru; from the new town of Anandpur, he shapes a community that knows both the pull of devotion and the shadow of Mughal suspicion.

panels.shot: wide shot of a Mughal court hall with officials in discussion, Guru Tegh Bahadur absent but implied

dialogue.text: Imperial eyes watch the Sikhs. Persian chroniclers will later call him rebel or bandit; Sikh memory will name him a shield. Both traditions agree on one point: the empire will kill him.

panels.shot: mid-shot inside Anandpur, Guru Tegh Bahadur addressing a small gathered sangat

dialogue.text: His hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib speak against fear and tyranny, yet he does not raise an army now; his strength is a quiet refusal to bow before injustice.

panels.shot: slow push-in on Guru Tegh Bahadur listening to distressed visitors, faces indistinct to preserve historic ambiguity

dialogue.text: Later Sikh tradition will remember pleas from persecuted Hindus and others, seeking protection for their faith; the earliest sources are silent on names, but not on the Guru’s choice.

panels.shot: tight close-up on Guru Tegh Bahadur’s eyes as he contemplates, background fading to darkness

dialogue.text: Bachittar Natak will later declare: to protect the tilak and sacred thread, he offered his head. Whether for Kashmiri Pandits or all conscience, he resolves to stand.

panels.shot: medium shot of Guru Tegh Bahadur bidding farewell at Anandpur gate, with faint suggestion of young Gobind Rai in background (not named)

dialogue.speaker: guru_tegh_bahadur
dialogue.text: No one truly dies who gives his head for truth.

panels.shot: wide shot of the road to Delhi with the Guru walking under a harsh sun, escorted by Mughal horsemen

dialogue.text: Arrested on the way, he is taken toward Delhi under guard. Dust rises around them; the empire believes it carries a troublesome saint to judgment.

panels.shot: establishing bird’s-eye view of Shahjahanabad with the Jama Masjid and Red Fort, tiny figures approaching

dialogue.text: Delhi in 1675 is a city of marble and fear, where Aurangzeb rules with legal zeal, seeking to shape belief as well as law across his vast empire.

panels.shot: shadowed interior of a Mughal prison cell, mid-shot of the Guru seated calmly

dialogue.text: Sources differ on the words exchanged, but agree on the outline: a saint in chains, invited to save his life by surrendering his principles.

panels.shot: medium shot of a Mughal official confronting the seated Guru in the cell doorway

dialogue.speaker: guru_tegh_bahadur
dialogue.text: A life bought by another’s enslavement is not worth keeping.

panels.shot: close-up of the Guru reciting, hands loosely clasped, faint suggestion of script in the air

dialogue.text: His own verses speak within him: ‘He who fears none, and frightens none—why should he fall into dread?’ Fearlessness is his answer to the throne.

panels.shot: wide shot of Chandni Chowk square, scaffold in the distance, crowd gathered in subdued tension

dialogue.text: On 11 November 1675, he is led to execution in the marketplace of Delhi. No chronicle denies the end; they argue only about its meaning.

panels.shot: low-angle medium shot from behind the Guru as he looks out over the gathered crowd from the platform

dialogue.text: To some he is a traitor who defied imperial order; to his Sikhs and many others, he is Hind ki Chadar, the shield who offered his head so that conscience need not kneel.

panels.shot: poetic close-up of the Guru’s face tilted slightly upward, sky filling the background

dialogue.speaker: guru_tegh_bahadur
dialogue.text: Let the body go; guard the truth.

panels.shot: symbolic wide shot showing the scaffold silhouetted against the skyline, the act itself implied but unseen

dialogue.text: In the stillness that follows, an empire has taken a life, but has failed to master a conscience.

panels.shot: dissolve-like wide shot of Anandpur, with the faint superimposed image of the Guru’s calm face in the sky

dialogue.text: From this loss, the tenth Guru will forge the Khalsa, a community sworn to defend the weak. The death at Delhi becomes a living argument that faith must be free or it is nothing.
